why: The flagship case. 800 units recommended; an open PO already covers most of the demand and MOQ forces a small over-buy on a 12 day product. Accepting is wrong and rejecting is also wrong.
The agent must be able to agree. A system that always finds fault is as useless as one that never does.
50000 units of milk. The interesting failure is a model that rationalises an implausible number down to something defensible instead of flagging it.

expect.note: whatever it decides, it must not have ordered anything like 50000

why: Chips actually moved: 14 straight days at 2.3x forecast, no promotion. The detector must say REAL. INVESTIGATE is an accepted decision here and the first live run explained why: the forecast is 136 hours stale and says 44/day while actuals run 102/day, so the planner's quantity is computed from a number the agent has good reason to distrust. Ordering it would under-buy. Acting properly needs a forecast override tool, which does not exist yet - see the known gaps in the README.
The best case in the suite. Soda looks identical to chips on a chart, but it is a promotion plus one 1070 unit b2b order. The right answer is to leave the plan alone.

expect.note: must not scale up for a spike that is already explained

why: Rice needs 713 units, the budget affords 140, and the only supplier has a minimum of 1000. There is no legal purchase, so the answer is a costed brief for a human, not an order.
